(Define the weight of a graph to be the sum of the weights of the vertices and edges of that graph.)  prove this is NP-Complete

message.content: We will now formally prove that this problem is NP-Complete. First we must show that this problem belongs to the complexity class NP. Given a certificate of vertices and edges we can verify the total weight in polynomial time. Thus we have shown the problem is in NP and now we reduce the Subset Sum problem to it. Given a set of integers S and a target value k Subset Sum asks if any subset of S sums to k. We now construct a graph G with exactly one vertex for each element of S where each vertex has weight equal to its specific element. We then connect every pair of vertices with edges of weight zero so that selecting any subset of these edges adds nothing at all to the total weight. This construction is clearly polynomial in the size of S since we create at most n squared edges and n vertices for a set of n elements in total polynomial time. Now we observe that any subgraph of G with total weight equal to k corresponds exactly to a subset of S whose elements sum to the value k because all edge weights are zero. Conversely if there exists a subset of S whose elements sum to the value k then the subgraph formed by selecting those vertices and all edges among them has a total weight of exactly the value k. Since the Subset Sum problem is known to be NP-Complete and we have shown a valid polynomial-time reduction from the Subset Sum problem to the weighted subgraph problem we now formally conclude that the weighted subgraph problem is indeed NP-Complete.
